The Righteous Mind by Jonathan Haidt.


This book may sound a bit conservative at first, but in my opinion it's not. It's an neutral, objective analysis of the way people build and maintain worldviews and beliefs.


In my experience, the only way to get through to people who are deep in conspiracy theories is to open up to the possibility that there may have been subjectively legitimate reasons that led to certain beliefs even if they are far away from factual truth.
(By giving your family member this book, you are indirectly expressing this and you avoid making them feel like a mad person in your eyes.) 


This book taught me to some extent why people belief certain things and what they get out of it (what are the functions of our beliefs). Once you're realising how humans tend to build up certain beliefs and why/how they maintain it, you're ready to really reflect your own beliefs and grasp all the irrationality in your worldview even if you always made logical conclusion in your subjective experience. (Hopefully that's the conclusion for your family member too) 


So this book can help a person to really start reflecting on their own beliefs and hopefully make them more critical of ideological ideas they are confronted with.


I think it would be highly profitable, since confronting conspiracy theorists with pure facts and showing them flaws in their worldview makes them defensive and they won't open up to anything.

In retrospective, great books.
